title: The fading in India
hookLine: Buddhism slowly waned in India; historians give many reasons and still debate them

cards: "All created things perish." That is the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, and the texts don't exempt the teaching itself. In one sutta the Buddha speaks plainly about a time when the true teaching could disappear.

In India, where he walked and taught, the monasteries did grow quiet. Not in a day: slowly, over generations, region by region, the robes and the chanting thinned out in many places where they had once been common.
Ask why, and you won't get one answer.

teach.b: First, the monasteries. In its later centuries in India, much of Buddhist life gathered in large monasteries supported by kings and wealthy donors.
Some historians suggest that when that support shifted, the monasteries had fewer roots in village life to fall back on. Second, the neighbors.
Hindu devotional movements grew strong in the same regions, and some Buddhist images, ideas and holy places were drawn into the wider religious life around them.
Some Hindu texts came to count the Buddha himself among the forms of Vishnu. Historians describe a slow blending, not a single moment. Third, violence.
Raids sacked great monasteries and scattered their monks. That is tomorrow's story. Fourth, the debate itself.
Historians weigh these reasons differently, and they are still arguing. Some stress the raids; others stress the long, quiet changes before them.
Some point out that the story differs region by region, and that the practice never vanished entirely.

So the honest summary is today's line: many reasons. The sutta offers a view from inside the tradition. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha says the true teaching is not made to disappear by earth, water, fire or wind.

It fades when a counterfeit of the teaching appears, the way real gold disappears from the world once counterfeit gold appears, and when people lose respect for the teacher, the teaching, the community, the training and concentration.
Some Buddhist teachers read that passage as a warning to look first at themselves, not at outside causes.

how: Buddhist teachers often read the passages about the decline of the true teaching as a call to keep their own practice sincere, and historians of India continue to study and debate why Buddhism faded there.

games.why: historians point to shifting royal support, the growth of devotional movements, and the raids, and they still argue about which mattered most.

practice: Bring to mind something that faded, a custom in your family, a language a grandparent spoke, a place that closed its doors, and hold it the way you'd hold something fragile, without explaining it or assigning blame.
On each out-breath, let it be what it is: something that mattered, and changed.

wordCard.voice: Saddhamma. The true teaching, which a sutta says fades not from fire or flood but when respect for it is lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: saddhamma, the true teaching, whose fading the sutta describes.
